title: UPDATE: Samsung Forecasts Long-Term Deals May Cover Up to 70% of Memory Production Through 2030

tickers.name: Alphabet Inc. Class A Common Stock
Alibaba Group Holding Limited American Depositary Shares, each represents eight Ordinary Shares

summary:
The Seoul-based chipmaker has entered into server memory supply agreements with 10 of its largest clients and is currently in talks with an additional 10. Samsung stated that based on current trends, it is increasingly likely that 60% to 70% of its total production capacity will be bound by these long-term contracts through 2030.

This shift toward extended agreements comes as hyperscalers seek to secure the DDR5 and LPDDR5 memory required for expanding AI infrastructure. While industry supply deals typically last three to five years, cloud providers including Alibaba, Tencent, and ByteDance have sought contracts reaching through 2035. Similar discussions involving Google suggest a broader move by tech giants to lock in volumes and prioritize supply stability over the memory market's traditional pricing cycles.

selectedTweets.text:
According to Korean media, $BABA, Tencent and ByteDance are asking Samsung and SK Hynix for long term server memory supply deals.

The normal length of these contracts is 3 to 5 years.

Some of the Chinese companies want 10 YEAR deals that run all the way to 2035.

They want server DDR5 and LPDDR, including the low power memory used to make AI servers more efficient.

This comes after the biggest United States tech companies already locked in their own supply through long term agreements.

The Chinese buyers are reportedly willing to accept higher prices just to secure the volume.

When the largest buyers in the world are trying to lock up memory for a decade, that tells you how tight this market really is.
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
The memory shortage could get MUCH worse in 2027.

According to Dell's CEO, the memory shortage isn't going away anytime soon. In fact, he expects it to get worse in 2027 because building a new memory fabrication plant takes roughly four years. And this is exactly why I've been so bullish on the memory trade. Demand for DRAM, NAND, and HBM continues to increase as hyperscalers aggressively expand their AI infrastructure, but manufacturers cannot simply bring new capacity online overnight. Even with billions being invested into expanding production, much of that additional capacity won't be available for several years.

Meanwhile, AI inference and agentic workloads are creating entirely new sources of memory demand beyond just training larger models. As these systems become more sophisticated, they require more memory to handle larger context windows, store information, and process increasingly complex workloads. And remember, it's not just AI companies competing for this supply. Traditional data centers, smartphones, PCs, and enterprise servers still need memory, which means manufacturers have to balance growing AI demand with the rest of the market. This is why I believe the current memory cycle could last much longer than previous cycles. If Michael Dell is right and shortages worsen in 2027, we could see memory pricing remain elevated, stronger margins for manufacturers, and potentially a much longer earnings growth cycle than investors are currently pricing in. I still believe memory is one of the most underrated opportunities in the entire AI infrastructure trade.
